directions.novelty_line: **Novelty:** partly new. Published work already shows that a model one tier down from the top forecasts research results about as well as the top one, and that much smaller models do worse. BrainBench (Luo et al., 2024, arXiv 2403.03230; Nature Human Behaviour) found that 7B models "performed comparably to larger models", while TinyLlama (1.1B) was "falling much behind the 7B models". SciPredict (arXiv 2604.10718, 2026) has Claude Sonnet 4.5 at 22.55% against Opus 4.5 at 23.05% and Llama 3.1 8B at 14.65%. Hewitt et al. (2024, working paper) found that accuracy "improved steadily and markedly across generations of LLMs". Ours agrees on the size pattern: Sonnet is not shown different from Opus (Brier 0.168 against 0.163; paired difference +0.004, interval −0.018 to +0.027) and Haiku is weaker (0.208; paired difference from Opus +0.044, interval +0.012 to +0.076). What we found in no paper is a test of a same-family smaller model against a publication-bias rule ("bet on the paper's good-news side") or a "which version flatters the paper" rater. Wen et al. (2025, arXiv 2506.00794) do not mention publication bias, and CUSP (Wu et al., 2026, arXiv 2605.22681) has always-No, chance and mean-date baselines but no publication-bias one; Jin et al. (2024, arXiv 2411.17595) found GPT-4o-mini predicting every clinical trial a success, a smaller same-family model collapsing onto a positive-outcome rule, but report no such rule as a baseline. So the result that Haiku beats a coin but is not shown to beat the good-news rule by the 0.01 margin, and that neither smaller model beats the flattery rater on round 2's items (a reported row), is new. directions.novelty_line: **Novelty:** new. No published work I found reports that a valence question ("which version is better news for the paper's own idea?") solves BrainBench or any real-versus-altered results task. BrainBench (Luo et al., 2024, arXiv 2403.03230, *Nature Human Behaviour*) ran local-context, swapped-sentence, zlib-perplexity memorisation, publication-date, calibration and GPT-4-item controls, and found "no indication that BrainBench was memorized". It tests no valence, positive-result or publication-bias shortcut, and neither do its follow-ups (Luo, Sun and Love, 2024, arXiv 2405.09395; Luo, Ramscar and Love, 2024, arXiv 2411.11061) or Wen et al. (2025, arXiv 2506.00794, which checks "superficial features like idea complexity"). Lee (2026, arXiv 2604.06236) is not this test, and it does not mention BrainBench, valence or shortcuts. It proposes, without running anything (§5.5: "does not include empirical validation"), three things. §4.1: give LLMs only the starting information of 200–500 completed ClinicalTrials.gov trials, ask for a probability of success, and score with AUC-ROC and with the probabilities given to failed trials, hypothesising that "LLMs systematically overestimate the probability of experimental success". §4.2: compare five context conditions (none, successes only, failures only, both, failures classified by cause), with a dose-response at 10, 50, 100 and 200 failure records. §5.3: correlate "the published positive-result ratio and the actual success ratio (obtainable from trial registries)" across medical subfields, plus a peer-review test on OpenReview. So this project's earlier statement that ours is "the test an April 2026 paper asked for" (paper/novelty.md finding 8, ranked replication 1) overstates the link. The swap-both-orders-and-average fix and the first-position pull are known: Zheng et al. (2023, arXiv 2306.05685) found Claude-v1 consistent on swapped order 23.8% of the time and favouring the first answer 75.0%; Wang et al. (2023, arXiv 2305.17926, Balanced Position Calibration) average the scores over both orders. LLMs swayed by favourable framing is in print in another form (Yun et al., CHIL 2025, arXiv 2502.07963, spin in medical abstracts), but not as a rule for picking real results. What is new is only the headline, a one-line valence question beating the 63.4% for experts on BrainBench, and it cannot be told apart from memory or plausibility. Search: "BrainBench" with shortcut, valence, positive result, publication bias, memorization, contamination, follow-up; "LLMs predict scientific results publication bias"; "LLM spin medical abstracts"; "position bias swap LLM judge"; general web search and arxiv.org abstract and HTML pages, 2026-11-05. (2024, arXiv 2403.03230 v4, *Nature Human Behaviour*) prompted no model for an answer: "A correct response was when the model produces a lower perplexity for the original abstract than the altered abstract", each abstract prefixed only with "You are a neuroscientist with deep knowledge in neuroscience", on open models only (Llama-2 7B to 70B and chat, Mistral-7B and instruct, Falcon-40B and 180B and their instruct/chat versions, Galactica 6.7B to 120B, TinyLlama 1.1B, Phi-3 3.8B, GPT-2 trained from scratch, BrainGPT; GPT-4 only wrote the 100 extra items, and Claude is not mentioned); it reports "LLMs averaging 81.4% accuracy and human experts averaging 63.4%", Phi-3 the best named model at 82.5%, and BrainGPT 3% above its base model. Its controls were local context only, swapped sentences, zlib-perplexity memorisation ("no indication that BrainBench was memorized"), publication date, calibration and the GPT-4-written items; it ran none for valence, flattery, positive results or option order (perplexity scores each version on its own), and it avoided prompting because "Prompting in natural language may yield less reliable judgments and degrade model competency", having found that "Chat or instruction-optimized models performed worse than their base model counterparts". The kind of result is in print elsewhere: Chen, Hu and Lu (2025, arXiv 2504.01167) prompted GPT-3.5, GPT-4-turbo and GPT-4o to pick a real field-experiment conclusion from among itself, a reversed variant and an unrelated variant (best 78%, GPT-4o with chain of thought), and found that the conclusion's sentiment label predicted accuracy only in interaction with some topics (for example ethnicity); Liu and Shah (2023, arXiv 2306.00622) found GPT-4 "biased towards the abstract that has a positive (p<0.05) result" in one constructed pair; and in metascience terms, Fanelli (2012, *Scientometrics* 90:891–904) found that 85.9% of 2007 papers that tested a hypothesis reported support for it, a base rate a "better news" rule could exploit. No paper found reports a prompted Claude or GPT-4-class model on BrainBench, a valence-only question solving a real-versus-altered results task, or that question's gap to a direct forecasting prompt; so what is new here is only that comparison: Opus 89.4% with the valence question and 95.2% asked directly, with a similar gap on Sonnet (+6.3 points) and one not shown on Haiku (+5.3, interval including zero). This disagrees with ss-b10c's "new", whose search missed Chen et al., and it cannot separate valence from memory or plausibility. Search: "BrainBench" with GPT-4o, Claude, o1, prompted, shortcut, heuristic, follow-up; "LLM predict experimental outcomes optimism bias positive results"; "frontier models real versus altered paper result"; "LLM hypothesis-supporting abstract publication bias"; "LLM forecast replication outcomes positive results cue metascience"; Fanelli "Negative results are disappearing"; general web search (standard and extended) and arxiv.org search for "BrainBench", with full text read of arXiv 2403.03230v4 (HTML), 2504.01167v3 (HTML), 2306.00622 (PDF) and Fanelli 2012 (PDF), 2026-11-05. directions.novelty_line: **Novelty:** partly new. Luo et al. (2024, arXiv 2403.03230v4, *Nature Human Behaviour*) scored 15 open-weight models (Galactica 6.7B, 30B and 120B; Falcon-40B and 180B; Llama-2 7B, 13B and 70B; Mistral-7B; base and chat or instruct versions; GPT-2, TinyLlama, Phi-3 and their LoRA-tuned BrainGPT in the supplement) by the perplexity of each abstract, each scored on its own under one fixed prefix ("You are a neuroscientist with deep knowledge in neuroscience. Here is an abstract from a neuroscience publication:"). Its controls were local context only, results sentences swapped within a subfield, memorisation (zlib-perplexity ratio against a Gettysburg Address anchor, publication date against difficulty), calibration, and items written by GPT-4; it asked no model a question in words ("Our approach diverged from the popular approach of prompting models for responses through natural language"), so it ran no valence or flattery question, no option-order test and no second prompt wording, and it tested no Claude or other closed model. The kind of result is in print: Hua et al. (2025, arXiv 2509.01790; 7 LLMs, 6 benchmarks, 12 templates) trace much prompt sensitivity to log-likelihood scoring and rigid answer matching, with "a substantial reduction in performance variance" when an LLM judge reads the answers, which agrees with our near-equal totals; JudgeSense (Bellibatlu, Raff and Zhang, 2026, arXiv 2604.23478v3; 25 judges including claude-haiku-4-5 and claude-sonnet-4-5) finds "rewording moves a judge's verdict by more than its own decoding noise does", the pattern in Haiku's item scores (70.5% the same against an 81.8% noise floor), though on its two pairwise tasks the cost did not clear its threshold; Mizrahi et al. (2024, arXiv 2401.00595) and Sclar et al. (2023, arXiv 2310.11324; up to 76 accuracy points from formatting, LLaMA-2-13B, few-shot) report larger brittleness elsewhere. Nearest on the task, Chen, Hu and Lu (2025, arXiv 2504.01167) carried Luo's real-versus-reversed design to 1,261 conclusions from 276 field experiments on GPT models and found that conclusion sentiment, interacting with topic, predicted accuracy, but they asked which conclusion is true, not which flatters the authors; in metascience terms, Fanelli (2012, *Scientometrics* 90:891) found 85.9% of papers that tested a hypothesis in 2007 reported support for it, the base rate that would let "pick the version better for the authors' idea" beat chance, yet no paper found tests that rule on a real-versus-altered task, or its robustness to a second wording, which is what this bet adds.
